newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian gold shake-up positive but no panacea.
newsitem.headline: Russian gold shake-up positive but no panacea.

text.p: Plans to overhaul Russia's cumbersome, Soviet-era gold market are aimed at attracting commercial banks and their capital clout but offer no panacea for the struggling system, industry sources said on Friday.
First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said radical changes were needed to the gold market and added that concrete steps towards creating a free market would be presented to him within 10 days.
"A greater role for private banks will be a part of the plan which we are preparing now," said Vladimir Rybkin, head of the Finance Ministry's precious metals and stones section.
"The main aim of the plan is to develop the gold producing industry and attract to it additional investment."
Commercial banks are already a growing force in Russian gold, which cash-strapped Moscow can ill afford to support.
The government borrowed 2.8 trillion roubles ($490 million) from commercial banks this year to give to Russian gold miners as advance payments to finance output.
Central Bank sources said the banks' role was bound to grow under planned changes.
At the moment, all direct purchases from gold producers are centralised and the government has tight control over exports.

Bullion analysts said commercial banks' ascendancy in Russian gold would be good for the industry in the long term, although it would take time before liberalisation reverses the downward production trend in recent years.

"There is a lot of gold out there, so I would have thought by definition that if they improve the financing of the sector then it will help production-wise," said Rhona O'Connell, metals markets analyst at T.Hoare and Co in London.
Russian gold production estimates for last year varied widely between 101 and 124 tonnes against a range of 108 to 135 in 1995. Production was 150 tonnes as recently as 1993.
Industry officials in Russia have said that gold production could be doubled if the right reforms were introduced. But analysts believe that any major output recovery would be slow.
"For a start there is a five year lead time for greenfield operations," O'Connell said.
And production was not only dictated by credit for hundreds of mining enterprises, but also by geological factors.

Andy Smith, precious metals analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) in London, said about 75 percent of Russian output comes from alluvial, surface mines, while 75 percent of its gold reserves lay in hard-rock, underground deposits.
"A change from one to the other means capital -- market liberalisation must at least lubricate that geological change," he said.
Smith added that the Russian government appreciated the enormity of the task of gold market reform, which is bound to involve social as well as industrial costs.
"Change is not going to happen overnight and I don't think that the Russians have any illusions that this (liberalisation) is a magic wand," he said.
Other proposals under consideration reform include industry consolidation, partly through merging smaller mining operations, Rybkin said.
"We have this aim as well - it is especially hard for smaller companies to work (under the current system)."
Banks proved ready lenders of cheap credit to the government in February in a sign they were jockeying for position ahead of full liberalisation.
In return for their generosity, banks are likely to demand a say in the sensitive world of gold exports, analysts said.
"The key thing is that commercial banks would have to be given enough freedom to export the gold if they wanted," a Western bullion analyst said.
